text: The previous lesson showed three parts inside the pot.
title: Recall the root zone

text: Name these parts before the answer appears.
title: Name the three parts

text: The three parts are solid material, water, and air.
title: Solids, water and air

visual.alt: Ten equal total volumes: six water, two solid material and two air. A 60% VWC example.

text: Think of ten equal boxes making up the whole sample. How many boxes worth of water are inside it? That is the idea behind volumetric water content, or VWC: water volume divided by total sample volume, shown as a percentage.
title: What VWC measures

visual.alt: Ten equal total volumes: six water, two solid material and two air. A 60% VWC example.

text: In the drawing, water takes up six of the ten equal volumes. Six divided by ten is zero point six. Multiply by one hundred: sixty percent.
title: Six out of ten

visual.alt: Ten equal total volumes: six water, two solid material and two air. A 60% VWC example.

text: The blocks make the arithmetic visible. In real substrate, that water is spread through spaces between solid parts. It does not sit in six separate water blocks.
title: A ratio, not separate blocks

visual.alt: Ten equal total volumes: six water, two solid material and two air. A 60% VWC example.

text: Use a larger example: a total substrate sample of five litres at sixty percent VWC. Five times zero point six is three, so this sample contains three litres of water.
title: Water already in the sample

text: Imagine labelling the sample: three litres of water already inside. That label is not a watering instruction. It does not tell you to pour another three litres into a five litre pot.
title: Existing water, not an added dose

text: Sixty percent of the total volume is water. Is all the remaining forty percent air?
title: What is in the other 40%?

visual.alt: One probe samples a local region, not every pot.

text: No. The remaining volume includes solid material and air. VWC alone does not give the complete air volume.
title: The remainder includes solids

labels: VWC does not give air volume
visual.alt: One probe samples a local region, not every pot.

text: Do not read VWC like a fuel gauge showing how much usable fuel remains. Water in substrate is not all equally easy for roots to take up. Some is held more tightly. The same VWC in different substrates can mean different conditions for the plant.
title: VWC is not a fuel gauge

visual.alt: One probe samples a local region, not every pot.

text: Look at the probe. Its position and contact with the substrate matter. Calibration means checking how its output relates to the quantity being measured. These things affect whether the local reading is trustworthy.
title: The probe samples one region

visual.alt: One probe samples a local region, not every pot.

text: A probe near one dripper might not represent a dry pot at the end of a row. Later lessons explain how to select locations that represent the zone.
title: Check beyond the nearest dripper

labels: A distant pot may be dry
visual.alt: One probe samples a local region, not every pot.

text: The sensor now shows forty percent VWC. Does this reading always mean that the substrate is too dry?
title: Does 40% always mean too dry?

text: No. Forty percent in one substrate can mean something different in another. Use your substrate, checked reference values, crop and current conditions to interpret it. There is no single VWC target for every system.
title: A target needs local evidence

text: Do not select a target yet. Complete this sentence. Sixty percent VWC means what?
title: Explain 60% VWC

text: Approximately sixty percent of the measured sample volume is water. This is one correct answer.
title: 60% of measured sample volume

text: The reading does not give the exact water volume available to the plant. One sensor does not prove that all pots have the same conditions.
title: Know what the reading cannot prove

labels: Not every pot in the zone

text: Use these limits when you assess advice about VWC.
title: Check the meaning of VWC advice

text: Next, a kitchen sponge will help explain saturation, water left after drainage, and the reference number in the app.
title: Next: when is a pot full?

text: Dunk a kitchen sponge, then lift it out, dripping. Water fills the spaces inside it. Picture that as saturation.
title: Dunk the sponge

visual.alt: Let excess water drain without squeezing. Water remains and air returns to some spaces.

text: The sponge material has not vanished. In substrate, water also fills spaces between solids. Saturation does not mean one hundred percent of the total sample is water.
title: The solid material stays

visual.alt: Let excess water drain without squeezing. Water remains and air returns to some spaces.

text: Hold the sponge over the sink. Do not squeeze it. Let the excess water drip away. It still feels wet, but some spaces now contain air again.
title: Let excess water drip

visual.alt: Let excess water drain without squeezing. Water remains and air returns to some spaces.

text: Soaked and dripping, then wet after drainage: those are two different conditions. The same distinction matters in a pot, where roots need both water and oxygen.
title: Two wet conditions

visual.alt: Let excess water drain without squeezing. Water remains and air returns to some spaces.

text: Now wet a spare container of substrate. Let excess water drain using a suitable, repeatable check. Do not squeeze the substrate.
title: Now check the container

visual.alt: Conceptual container cutaway: excess water drains; water and air remain among solids.

text: The water left after that check is its container capacity: water held under those particular container and drainage conditions.
title: Water left after the check

visual.alt: Conceptual container cutaway: excess water drains; water and air remain among solids.

text: Tall and shallow containers can retain different amounts. Substrate matters too. One sponge cannot tell you what every pot holds.
title: Your container matters

visual.alt: Conceptual container cutaway: excess water drains; water and air remain among solids.

text: This drainage check describes container capacity. The app also has a field capacity reference. Check how it is set: automatic updates can follow observed wet peaks. A wet peak alone is not a drained-container measurement.
title: The program says field capacity

text: Repeat with the same substrate, container, starting condition and drainage procedure. There is no single drainage time for every setup.
title: Repeat the same conditions

visual.alt: Conceptual container cutaway: excess water drains; water and air remain among solids.

text: Check probe placement and contact. Compare its reading with container weight and drainage. A number alone cannot show that the check worked.
title: Compare reading and reality

visual.alt: Placement and contact matter; compare with appropriate independent evidence.

text: Example: a one litre total substrate sample contains six hundred millilitres of water. Six hundred divided by one thousand is sixty percent VWC: volumetric water content.
title: A concrete VWC example

text: Imagine writing that sixty percent on a Post-it beside the sponge. Changing the Post-it to seventy percent would not add a drop of water.
title: The Post-it cannot wet it

visual.alt: An unchanged wet sponge beside a reference note. A software reference cannot add water.

text: The app reference works like that note. It tells the program which number to use. The edit itself adds no water.
title: The app is a reference note

visual.alt: The note now reads 70%. Editing it adds no water to the unchanged sponge.

text: You change the app reference from sixty to seventy percent. What happens to the water already in the pot?
title: Pause and think

text: Nothing. You changed the note, not the water. A physical change needs water to enter or leave.
title: Nothing happens to the water

visual.alt: The note now reads 70%. Editing it adds no water to the unchanged sponge.

text: And sixty percent was only our worked example. Your own container check could give a different result.
title: Example, not a target

labels: Your pot needs its own check

text: The highest spike on a graph is not automatically the drained reference. It could be a brief wet peak or a bad reading.
title: A peak is not a container check

text: Think back to the sponge: dripping wet, then wet after excess water drains, then a note describing it.
title: Remember the sponge

visual.alt: Let excess water drain without squeezing. Water remains and air returns to some spaces.

text: The first two describe physical conditions. The note, like the app setting, describes a reference supported by a suitable check.
title: Condition and description

visual.alt: An unchanged wet sponge beside a reference note. A software reference cannot add water.

text: Next comes dryback: water content falls as water leaves. Keep the sponge and its Post-it separate mentally.
title: Next: water content falls

text: Think of a car dashboard: the speedometer and fuel gauge share one panel, but tell you different things. This graph puts water content and EC on one screen. We will learn what each line means.
title: Two gauges, one screen

text: Read time along the bottom, like a diary laid out from left to right. Farther right means later. The shaded section is night in this example. The sensors can keep measuring through it.
title: Read time from left to right

text: Start with the blue line: VWC, or water content by volume. Read its height against the percentage scale on the left. Use the time below to find when that reading happened.
title: VWC uses the left scale

text: At this example point, the reading is sixty percent VWC. The solid line joins the observations so you can follow the change over time.
title: Read the point at its time

text: A stale weather report cannot tell you the weather now. Check the age of live readings and look for missing sections. A smooth-looking line does not prove fresh, complete measurements.
title: Check reading age and gaps

text: Imagine a tiny electrical test through a sample. Dissolved salts help carry the current. EC, electrical conductivity, measures how readily current passes. Read EC on the right-hand scale, in millisiemens per centimetre.
title: EC: how readily current passes

text: Before interpreting EC, ask where it was measured. A number from the tank does not automatically describe the water around the roots.
title: Which EC measurement is shown?

text: Feed EC describes the irrigation solution. Bulk substrate EC measures the combined substrate region. Pore-water EC describes water in the spaces between solids. These are different measurements; identify which one your graph actually shows.
title: Where was EC measured?

text: Now the two lines cross on screen. Think of the speedometer needle and fuel-gauge needle pointing the same way. Would that make speed equal fuel? Do crossing VWC and EC lines mean equal measurements?
title: Crossing lines: equal measurements?

text: No. One uses percent on the left; the other uses conductivity units on the right. Their screen positions depend on those scales. Follow how each measurement changes over time.
title: Different units, different scales

text: Subtracting EC from VWC would be like subtracting litres from kilometres per hour. The quantities and units do not match. EC alone is not a complete nutrient recipe either.
title: Do not subtract unlike units

text: On this teaching chart, delivery markers show when watering started. In the app, a dot marks a shot start; a ring marks a shot the watering software held. Neither alone measures water delivered. VWC may rise after water reaches the probe, then fall between deliveries.
title: Find the irrigation event markers

labels: Water reaches the probe, then VWC rises

text: EC does not have to mirror VWC. Delivery, mixing, drainage, temperature, measurement method and crop conditions can affect it. Seeing two changes together does not prove that one caused the other.
title: EC has several influences

text: Think of a journey plan beside the trip you actually drove. The dashed planning reference comes from software settings. The measured line shows observations. They need different labels even if they happen to follow the same path.
title: The journey plan and the actual trip

text: Follow the planning line through the shaded night to the next morning. Like a route drawn on a map, it should be readable across the whole journey. A continuous line is still only a reference, not proof of tomorrow's crop response.
title: The reference continues through night

text: Here the EC reference joins the last daytime reference to the next morning reference. The overnight phase is called P3. This join is not a separately scheduled P3 EC target, and it does not calculate how salts will behave overnight.
title: Overnight EC is a reference connection

labels: EC reference joins day to morning
No separately scheduled P3 EC target

text: Now watch this demo edit. We increase the P3 emergency VWC threshold in the local draft. The draft threshold changes from thirty-five percent to thirty-nine percent. The saved threshold remains visible for comparison. The measured example readings remain the same.
title: Move only the draft threshold

text: Which item changed? The previous water content? The local draft of a threshold? Or a guaranteed irrigation event?
title: Which item changed?

text: Only the local draft changed. Think of a fridge alarm limit: it marks an exceptional condition, not the normal temperature you aim for. This emergency water threshold is not a normal overnight target. Review and apply are separate actions; the watering software, called the Controller, still checks its conditions and protection rules before irrigation.
title: An alarm limit is not a normal target

text: Point to the time axis. Point to the VWC scale. Point to the EC scale. Identify one irrigation marker. Identify one planning reference. Find the reading age.
title: Read the whole graph

text: The next lesson explains the irrigation phases from P0 to P3.
title: Next: irrigation phases

text: Start with one zone: plants whose water delivery is controlled together. Prove that small system works before expanding.
title: Start with one zone

text: Think of watering by hand: you need somewhere to make the plan, a way to check wetness, a water supply, a way to start and stop it, and checks against mistakes. An automated system needs those same five functions.
title: Five jobs, as with hand watering

text: Every app needs a computer to run on. Here that computer is called the host. Choose one supported route: a Raspberry Pi, or a dedicated Intel NUC or other x86-64 computer. You only need one.
title: Host means the computer

visual.alt: Pi OR dedicated x86-64: alternative host routes.

text: Like any computer, the host needs the correct power supply, suitable storage for its software and data, and a reliable network connection.
title: Provide the host essentials

visual.alt: Pi OR dedicated x86-64: alternative host routes.

text: The two host lessons are alternative routes to the same starting point. Follow the one for your chosen computer.
title: Two routes, one host choice

visual.alt: Pi OR dedicated x86-64: alternative host routes.

text: Think of labels on a switchboard: one label identifies a reading or a control. Home Assistant calls these named items entities. Crop Steering uses those entities. You need both the Crop Steering integration and the separate Controller app; a dashboard display alone cannot run irrigation. The integration holds room settings and the workspace. The Controller reads those settings and decides when to water.
title: Entities are named readings or controls

visual.alt: Conceptual information path from sensors through a compatible interface and Home Assistant to Crop Steering.

text: The moisture probe is the system's local wetness check. Choose a model suitable for the substrate and a position that represents the zone. Verify its exact model, connection interface and units, rather than buying on appearance.
title: Verify the moisture measurement path

labels: One probe cannot prove every pot
visual.alt: Conceptual information path from sensors through a compatible interface and Home Assistant to Crop Steering.

text: Some probes need a bridge: equipment that translates their connection into one the system can use. Matching wire colours do not prove compatibility. One working probe cannot prove equal delivery to every pot.
title: A bridge translates the connection

visual.alt: Conceptual information path from sensors through a compatible interface and Home Assistant to Crop Steering.

text: EC needs a location label too. Bulk substrate EC describes a measurement through the substrate region; pore-water EC describes the water between solids. Feed EC describes the solution supplied to the crop. Check what the sensor actually measures.
title: Identify the root-zone EC method

labels: Feed EC is a different measurement

text: A tank reading stays a tank reading when you rename its label. Calling feed EC root-zone EC cannot move the measurement into the pot.
title: Changing a label cannot move a reading

text: Air temperature and humidity help explain changing water demand, just as laundry dries differently on a hot, dry day than a cool, damp one.
title: Environment informs water demand

text: Trace water from its source, as you would trace a garden hose. A suitable pressurised supply may feed a zone valve directly. A reservoir needs a pump if it cannot provide the required pressure.
title: Choose the actual supply route

labels: Pump only when pressure requires it
visual.alt: An example irrigation path. Draw and verify the components actually installed in your setup.

text: Do not add a pump just because a diagram has one. If your water path requires a pump, include that pump and the protection suited to it.
title: Include the required pump protection

visual.alt: An example irrigation path. Draw and verify the components actually installed in your setup.

text: Follow the whole path: filtration, pressure regulation, drainage, and protection against reverse flow or unwanted siphoning. These must suit the actual equipment and meet applicable local requirements.
title: Design the complete water path

visual.alt: An example irrigation path. Draw and verify the components actually installed in your setup.

text: Starting a pump can demand more power than keeping it running, like the extra push needed to get a loaded trolley moving. Control hardware needs suitable starting and operating ratings and correct installation. A household smart plug's large printed rating alone does not prove suitability.
title: Control hardware must suit the load

text: Use an appropriately qualified installer for electrical work. Do not do mains electrical work as part of this course.
title: Electrical work needs an installer

labels: No mains work in this course

text: Two people turning the same tap can defeat each other's instructions. Give each physical pump or valve one controller. An old irrigation system must not also operate that output.
title: One tap, one controller

visual.alt: Verify one output owner and real stopping; a software state alone is insufficient.

text: Find and resolve competing control before enabling the new Controller.
title: Resolve shared control first

visual.alt: Verify one output owner and real stopping; a software state alone is insufficient.

text: The final function is protection and proof. Provide an accessible physical shutdown, suitable independent protection and somewhere safe to collect test water. Software OFF is like a stop request on a screen; it is not an emergency isolator.
title: Software OFF is not isolation

text: Use collection cups and a stopwatch to measure what actually arrives. Then observe the outlet after the stop command: the water must physically stop.
title: Measure delivery; prove stopping

text: A changed dashboard icon is a report from software. Look at the water outlet to prove stopping.
title: An icon is not physical proof

text: Build the basic working zone before adding instruments. Tank level, feed EC, pH, which describes acidity, and tank temperature add operating information. More probes and a verified flow meter can follow. Automated dosing, thermal cameras and artificial intelligence are not needed for the first working zone.
title: Add instruments after one proven zone

labels: Tank level · feed EC · pH · temperature
Later: more probes + verified flow meter

text: Sketch your water route like a simple road map. Label the supply, pump if installed, zone valve, drippers and drainage path.
title: Sketch a road map for the water

text: Beside that map, draw the probe and the Controller. Mark the physical shutdown and identify the one controller responsible for each output.
title: Separate measurement and control

text: Circle each item that you cannot identify.
title: Mark every unknown item

text: Check exact models using the equipment sheet before buying. Choose the host lesson for your Raspberry Pi or x86-64 computer.
title: Check models; choose one host route

text: Both host routes then join the same setup procedure: install one zone, assign its sensor readings and water controls, and verify physical operation before adding more zones.
title: Commission one zone before expanding
